summary: Discusses multihoming considerations for DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS), aiming to give guidance to DOTS clients and client-domain DOTS gateways that have more than one connection or provider. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If a house has two roads to the city, a call for help has to be sent the right way. This gives tips for asking for help against attacks when a network has several exits.

questions: how does dots work with multihoming
how should a dots client handle multiple providers
when should a dots client use anycast
subtitle: How to ask for DDoS help from multiple internet providers

tldr.problem: Networks with multiple internet connections need to signal DDoS attacks to the right provider. Sending help requests to an arbitrary provider will not mitigate the attack, and replicating all requests to all providers is inefficient.
tldr.mechanism: DOTS clients and gateways select the appropriate DOTS server based on the IP addresses under attack and the provider that owns them, avoiding anycast and ensuring the right provider receives the mitigation request.
tldr.outcome: Multihomed networks can now ask all their providers for help against attacks without confusing the request flow or wasting efforts on the wrong paths.

today: RFC 9284 is informational and provides guidance for deploying DOTS in multihomed networks. It complements the base DOTS protocols without requiring changes to them. It remains the reference for multihoming considerations in DOTS deployments.

sections.title: Introduction and DOTS Overview
sections.content:
DOTS (DDoS Open Threat Signaling) is a protocol that lets a network tell its internet service providers that it is under attack and needs help. DOTS clients signal attack information to DOTS servers run by upstream providers, which then activate mitigation.

This RFC adds guidance for networks that have multihoming: multiple connections to different providers or multiple paths through the same provider. The problem is that DOTS requests must go to the right provider. Sending a mitigation request to a provider that does not own the IP addresses being attacked wastes effort, and the attack traffic may still arrive on the unprotected path.

The RFC does not require changes to the base DOTS protocols (RFC 9132 and RFC 8783), only operational guidance on how to deploy them in multihomed settings.
sections.plainLanguage: DOTS is how you call the fire department when your network is on fire from attacks. But if you have two phone lines, you need to call the one your fire chief uses.

sections.title: Multihoming Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four multihoming scenarios, each with different constraints:

Residential CPE with multiple provisioning domains (fixed and mobile networks, often from the same provider) assigns Provider-Aggregatable (PA) addresses: the addresses belong to the provider and change per domain. A DOTS client on the CPE must contact the DOTS server associated with each domain and match each mitigation request to the provider that owns that target address.

Enterprise networks with a single CPE and multiple ISPs can use Provider-Independent (PI) addresses (owned by the enterprise itself) or PA addresses. With PI, the same address reaches any ISP but all ISPs must coordinate mitigation. With PA, requests must target the right ISP per address.

Enterprise networks with multiple CPEs and multiple ISPs need each CPE to handle its own DOTS gateways and upstream servers, with careful selection of which gateway reaches which server.

Multihomed enterprise with a single ISP offers simpler coordination: the single provider can use one DOTS server for all attachments, or separate servers that coordinate internally.
sections.plainLanguage: Some houses plug into one road, some into two roads. Some houses own the roads (PI), some rent them (PA). Different setups need different rules for which fire chief to call.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
For residential CPE, the DOTS client MUST establish and maintain sessions with all upstream DOTS servers because each server's mitigation scope is limited to its provisioning domain. The client MUST resolve the DOTS server name using DNS from the same domain and select source addresses according to RFC 6724 to ensure requests reach the correct server. Critically, the client MUST send a mitigation request to protect a target only to a DOTS server whose provider owns that target's IP addresses or prefix.

For enterprises with multiple clients and a single CPE gateway, the gateway can aggregate and relay requests from internal DOTS clients. With PA addresses, the gateway matches each request to the appropriate upstream server. With PI addresses or no filter rules, the gateway SHOULD relay to all DOTS servers. Anycast addressing is NOT RECOMMENDED because it does not guarantee the right server receives the request.

Enterprises with multiple CPEs should use per-CPE DOTS gateways. When PI addresses are in use, DOTS clients MUST contact all gateways simultaneously; anycast is again not recommended. When PA addresses are used with filter rules, clients select the gateway matching the target address.

For single-ISP multihoming, the enterprise may send requests to one or all attachments depending on its policy and the ISP's coordination capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: If you have two roads and one fire chief, call that chief. If you have two roads and two chiefs, both must know about the fire. Keep the address of the right chief with each road so you find them fast.

sections.title: Security and Information Leakage
sections.content:
DOTS clients should not leak information about attacks on one link to DOTS servers on different links that are not authorized to mitigate attacks for that link. If a DOTS client maintains per-link DOTS sessions, it should not share link-specific attack information with servers on unrelated links unless explicitly authorized by the domain administrator. The RFC notes that multihoming itself presents security threats (documented in RFC 4218), and DOTS clients inherit the security considerations of the base DOTS architecture (RFC 8811).

A DOTS client domain must decide whether to relax information isolation constraints and, if so, must explicitly configure that behavior under administrative control. Different deployment environments may require different policies; the RFC leaves this choice to the operator.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not tell one fire chief about a fire on a road his department does not serve. Tell only the chief who can help.
